content: Women who use Mirena are at an increased risk of experiencing a recurrence or reinfection of pelvic inflammatory disease (PID). Prior to insertion, all women must be informed about the potential for PID, which can lead to tubal damage, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, or, in rare cases, necessitate a hysterectomy or result in death. Patients should be educated to recognize and promptly report symptoms of PID to their physician. These symptoms include menstrual irregularities (such as prolonged or heavy bleeding), unusual vaginal discharge, abdominal or pelvic pain or tenderness, pain during intercourse (dyspareunia), chills, and fever. It is important to note that PID can sometimes be asymptomatic but still cause tubal damage and its associated complications. If PID is diagnosed or suspected, bacteriologic specimens should be collected, and antibiotic therapy should be initiated immediately. In most cases, removing Mirena after starting antibiotic treatment is appropriate. Guidelines for PID treatment are available from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) in Atlanta, Georgia. Actinomycosis has been associated with intrauterine devices (IUDs). Women with symptoms of actinomycosis who have an IUD should have the device removed and receive antibiotic treatment. However, the management of asymptomatic carriers is controversial, as actinomycetes can be part of the normal genital tract flora in healthy women without IUDs. False-positive findings of actinomycosis on Pap smears can occur, so it is recommended to confirm the diagnosis with cultures whenever possible. Mirena can alter bleeding patterns, leading to spotting, irregular bleeding, heavy bleeding, oligomenorrhea, or amenorrhea. During the first three to six months of use, the number of bleeding and spotting days may increase, and bleeding patterns may be irregular. Over time, the number of bleeding and spotting days typically decreases, but irregular bleeding may persist. If irregular bleeding develops during prolonged use, appropriate diagnostic measures should be taken to rule out endometrial pathology. Approximately 20% of Mirena users develop amenorrhea within one year. If menstruation does not occur within six weeks of the last menstrual period, pregnancy should be considered. Once pregnancy is excluded, repeated pregnancy tests are generally unnecessary in amenorrheic women unless other signs of pregnancy or pelvic pain are present. In women with heavy menstrual bleeding, the number of bleeding and spotting days may initially increase during the first months of therapy but usually decreases with continued use. The volume of blood loss per cycle progressively reduces over time. Mirena may become embedded in the myometrium, which can reduce its contraceptive effectiveness and result in pregnancy. An embedded Mirena should be removed, although removal may be difficult and, in some cases, require surgical intervention. Perforation or penetration of the uterine wall or cervix may occur during insertion, though it may not be detected until later. If perforation occurs, pregnancy may result. Mirena must be located and removed, and surgery may be required. Delayed detection of perforation can lead to migration outside the uterine cavity, adhesions, peritonitis, intestinal perforations, intestinal obstruction, abscesses, and erosion of adjacent organs. Clinical trials for Mirena excluded breastfeeding women. However, interim analysis from a large postmarketing safety study indicates an increased risk of perforation in lactating women. The risk of perforation may also be higher in women with a fixed retroverted uterus and during the postpartum period. To reduce the risk of perforation postpartum, Mirena insertion should be delayed for at least six weeks after delivery or until uterine involution is complete. If involution is significantly delayed, waiting until 12 weeks postpartum may be advisable. Insertion immediately after a first-trimester abortion does not appear to increase the risk of perforation, but insertion after a second-trimester abortion should be delayed until uterine involution is complete. Partial or complete expulsion of Mirena may occur. Symptoms of expulsion include bleeding or pain, but the device can also be expelled without the woman noticing, resulting in a loss of contraceptive protection. Partial expulsion may reduce Mirena's effectiveness. If menstrual flow increases after the first three to six months of use, expulsion should be considered. If expulsion has occurred, Mirena may be replaced within seven days of a menstrual period after ruling out pregnancy. Since Mirena's contraceptive effect is primarily local, ovulatory cycles with follicular rupture usually occur in women of reproductive age using Mirena. Occasionally, follicular atresia is delayed, and the follicle may continue to grow. Enlarged follicles have been diagnosed in approximately 12% of Mirena users. Most of these follicles are asymptomatic, but some may cause pelvic pain or dyspareunia. In most cases, the enlarged follicles resolve spontaneously within two to three months. Persistent enlarged follicles should be evaluated, though surgical intervention is rarely required. Women with current or past breast cancer, or those suspected of having breast cancer, should not use hormonal contraception, as breast cancer is a hormone-sensitive tumor. Spontaneous reports of breast cancer have been received during postmarketing experience with Mirena. However, because these reports are voluntary and come from a population of uncertain size, it is not possible to reliably estimate the frequency or establish a causal relationship to drug exposure. Two observational studies have not provided evidence of an increased risk of breast cancer during Mirena use. A complete medical and social history, including that of the partner, should be obtained to identify conditions that may influence the selection of an IUD for contraception. Mirena is contraindicated in women with a history of PID unless there has been a subsequent intrauterine pregnancy. A physical examination should include a pelvic exam, Pap smear, breast examination, and appropriate tests for sexually transmitted infections (e.g., gonorrhea and chlamydia) if indicated. Use of Mirena in patients with vaginitis or cervicitis should be postponed until the infection has been properly treated and eradicated, and it has been confirmed that the cervicitis is not due to gonorrhea or chlamydia. Irregular bleeding may obscure symptoms and signs of endometrial polyps or cancer.
